Hydriotaphia, Urne-Buriall, or, A Discourse of the Sepulchrall Urnes lately found in Norfolk is a work by the English polymath Thomas Browne , published in 1658 as the first part of a two-part work that concludes with The Garden of Cyrus .
The pretext for the book is the archaeological discovery of Anglo-Saxon pottery in Norfolk , with Browne describing the antiquities. He then provides a survey of funerary customs, both ancient and those current to his own era. In describing human nature , Browne notes the tendency of humans to solemnize both births and deaths, using their "pompous" graves to establish their self-importance .

Urn Burial

Literature by Thomas Browne

With a contribution by W.G. Sebald
Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial , is one of the pinnacles of Renaissance scholarship and without doubt one of the great essays in English literature. Beginning with observations on the recent discovery of Roman antiquities in the form of burial urns, Browne’s associative mind wanders to elephant graveyards, to pre-Christian cremation ceremonies, and finally to the idea of Christian burial. Browne then explores, with a more melancholic meditation, man’s struggles with mortality and the uncertainty of his fate and fame in the living world. This edition includes a magisterial discourse on Sir Thomas Browne taken from the first chapter of W. G. Sebald’s The Rings of Saturn .

(Short) Book Review: Urn Burial by Sir Thomas Browne

Let nothing remarkable escape us

Urn Burial is a strange and moody meditation on death and life centered around the discovery of human remains, Anglo-Saxons to be precise, buried in urns around Norfolk, England. It was written by Sir Thomas Browne and published in 1658. The full title is “Hydriotaphia, Urne-Burilall, or, A Brief Discourse of the Sepulchrall Urnes Lately Found in Norfolk.” Hydriotaphia means, in essence, “pot tomb” in Greek.
The book came to my attention after reading the odd and wonderful Rings of Saturn by W. G. Sebald, published in 1995. Sebald devotes a large portion of that book to a discussion of Urn Burial and Browne. That long section is excerpted in its entirety in the version of Urn Burial I read. It piqued my interest so I decided to read the original, and I’m glad I did.
It’s a short but powerful and memorable exploration of death and various funerary customs embedded in a morose contemplation of the fleeting nature of fame and life itself. Browne has a poetic writing style and a subversive sense of humor that serves the morbid topic well. The language is, naturally, dated but that only adds to the melancholy enjoyment.
